Every character in this film is a dickhead. Racist soldiers on the chopper? Dickheads. Spike Witwicky hawking his family airlooms for a car? Dickhead.  Spike Witwicky abandoning his friend at the lake? Double dickhead. Dad Witwicky taking his son to the Porsche garage? Dickhead. Mum Witwicky obsessed about her son gooning? Dickhead. Optimus Prime? Dickhead. Ironhide? Dickhead. John Turturro? Dickhead. Meghan Fox? Actually, not a dickhead, so Michael Bay got rid of her. There is something profoundly off in the writing of this movie. I feel it's like colourblind people trying to describe a colour they've never seen; in this case, it's facsimiles of human beings trying to write American teenagers and their relationships having only devoured other films about the topic. But there's something more than that - after all, Tarantino has made a career from refashioning the obsessions of his youth (and Bumblebee does a similar thing with more love and panache) - there's something profoundly off about all of the human characters in this film. It's vexing - if it had been slightly more surreal it might have ended up an almost Lynchian take on the psychosexual underbelly of teenage popular discourse, but we've arrived  here in this weird place by  accident, as jock writers do their best to embody pop cultural tropes that grow more distorted the more they are photocopied. But look, against my better judgement, once the movie stops pretending to be a John Hughes' dog in heat, it gets better. ILM absolutely smash the ball out the park and the back half is tight. I can just imagine Bay and the head of ILM doing that Arnold hand clasp from Predator before hitting the open air gym at Venice Beach once they'd locked the movie. Even though there are better live action versions of this that are roughly the same story (Bumblebee), movies that are just leagues better (TF:One, the original 86 film) and TV shows that have more pathos in their little cybertronian finger than this entire film (Animated, Prime, Seasons two and three of Cyberverse) I will admit that this is a singular vision, and you could not mistake it for the work of anyone else. A made-by-committee Marvel movie this is not. Only Michael Bay could have made this film, and he's probably a dickhead. It's definitely Michael Bay's world: your choice if you want to spend two hours in it.

Bon... Bah c'est d'la merde. Non, soyons sérieux : les effets visuels sont très réussis. Après, est-ce que ça suffit à en faire un bon film ? Spoiler : non. Le scénario est un pétard mouillé. Bon, ça c'est pas trop grave : je suis un des plus grands défenseurs de Pacific Rim, qui lui non plus ne brille pas par son scénario (quoique il maîtrise bien plus la caractérisation et le développement de ses personnages). Mais si en plus d'un scénario pourri digne des pires Emmerich, la mise en scène est pas ouf, bah ça devient vachement insipide. Et Michael Bay a beau faire plein de transformations de robots et une tonne d'explosion, ça ne fait ni chaud ni froid. Les personnages sont mal construits, la photo est laide, les couleurs sont délavées et m'ont rappelés Snyder (et ce n'est clairement pas un compliment), et en plus dans tout ça, Bay masque la médiocrité de sa mise en scène par des boum boum et des grosses voitures. Alors il y a quelques idées par-ci par-là, et certaines scènes d'action assez rigolotes, mais c'est jamais très impressionnant, jamais d'effet whaou, et dans un film qui pourtant n'a que ça pour briller, bah c'est très con. Ceci dit, et je conclurai là-dessus, c'est divertissant. Et ça je ne peux pas le reprocher à Michael Bay : c'est moche, c'est con, mais c'est rigolo.

Not as fun as I remember it being, just really meandering and boring and painfully juvenile. Which is obviously what you'd expect out of a Michael Bay movie, but not at all what I'm looking for given my current film taste. This movie has a similar problem to Masters of the Universe (2026), where it's got a strangely bloated runtime despite being based on a line of toys that are geared towards children. The plot of the movie is so simple that you could easily slice thirty, maybe even forty minutes off that runtime and still be left with a cohesive story. Also, it's actually kind of fascinating rewatching this as an adult with the retrospective awareness that this movie came out literally right in the middle of the Iraq War. This entire fucking movie literally feels like a glorified military advertisement.

I wish I had a polarizing take on Transformers (2007), but as a product of the 2000s, this had little impact on my life at a time that it very well could have. Some Michael Bay enthusiasts I know are unapologetically in love with the Transformers franchise, and I'll admit that I see the appeal. This is a bombastic, explosive, ten-toes-down blockbuster with commentary about military, police, and humanity, and it looks pretty great while doing it... but similarly to some of the Americanized Godzilla films, while I had a good time with this one, it failed to leave much of a lasting impression on me. I will give the film credit for its action sequences; it's over-the-top and impressive in its blockbuster filmmaking, especially for 2007. The CGI holds up refreshingly well, and the cliches aren't executed haphazardly. I think part of the disconnect comes from a lack of literacy in Bay's filmography, which I plan to rectify sooner rather than later, but I also struggle to reconcile that with the lack of humanity in the human characters. I found the Transformers themselves infinitely more interesting than Sam, Mikaela, or any of the other human characters. Sure, that's somewhat to be expected in the Transformers movie, but this 144-minute action extravaganza spent enough time on the humans to give me more meaningful time with them or more depth to the Transformers. I suppose I can find more of that in the next three films. Ultimately, I think there's room for me to appreciate this more on rewatch, but this is good, not great to my tastes as of today.

Tldr this would go so hard if I was 6 years old When Rachel told me tonight's movie was going to be Michael Bay's Transformers , I was a bit trepidatious. It's a bit of a cultural blind spot for me - I knew a lot about the film, I'd seen a lot of clips of Shia LaBeouf from the films, but never actually watched or engaged with anything from the Transformers franchise. Suffice to say it, the cultural footprint is familiar, even if the film itself was not. Over a pre-film game of catch, as if to underline the upcoming vibes, we heard the distant roar of a Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet, some miles away. That's not a regular occurrence in northwest London but today is apparent RAF day. Rachel was hyped, and she was hyping it up. We begin in a place that is absolutely Qatar. Why? Don't ask questions, enjoy the film. Things get messy real quick and I'll say this; this film looks fantastic. It is true what they say about CGI taking a step back since 2007. Maybe it's that there's just a lot going on or that the camera is always shaking: it doesn't matter, the decepticons, the autobots, and everything in between look probably exactly how you'd want them to look in a live-action film. Where were we? Ah yeah, havoc being wreaked on the US military industrial complex, getting steadily closer to home. Why is the little decepticon dude having an orgasm while he hacks? Freaky lil guy. Shia LaBeouf is easily the best part of this film, along with John Turturro. Genuinely funny, not necessarily served with the best writing, but gets an itchy energy that works really well for the film. I vaguely remember most of my school peers thirsting over Megan Fox in early secondary school. I get that, but her near-flawless conventional beauty doesn't make up for a total absence of acting talent. It becomes apparent that choices made by Michael Bay and the production team are designed to hide this with suggestive shots, and talk about engines that is never really truly about engines. This continues to a lesser extent as the film goes on. I worry these days that I'm too close to the action. I work semi-adjacently to defence, I play a lot of Arma, and I take an interest in geopolitics and defence policy. It's this knowledge that curses me, and forces me to sigh - yes, I know, it's a film about talking cars and vehicles from space - but if you're going to embrace the military industrial complex and essentially show off its power, you can't have A-10s go from dispatch to munitions delivery in 35 seconds (it's at least 35 minutes. At least ). The characterisation of some of these people is utterly diabolical, and almost certainly a product of the time. For example, there is 1 (one) black character who doesn't spend most lines of dialogue screaming/overreacting. Sam's parents must have been the inspiration for the Payday 3 security guards ("must have been the wind" ahhhh parents). But it's ok, the plot is shaky too. It's fine to begin with, but the plot holes come thick and fast, for example: - Sector 7 captures Sam and Mikaela and it's a big sad scene and everyone's angry at each other - it's the low point to end Act 2: but the next time we see them they're all chummy and gold and on a helicopter with the Secretary of Defence? Felt unearned. - We should keep Megatron under critical infrastructure, like the Hoover dam - President Hoover founded Sector 7, after all! - Wait, why has Secretary Voight gone with the hackers™ and John Turturro and hasn't got a platoon of security detail with him? He's the mf secretary of defence!!? - We need to get the allspice - sorry - the allspark away from here: let's go to a major population centre. Nothing bad has ever happened in a major population centre. - Every time Sam or Mikaela gets caught by one of the autobots after falling a height, that's gotta hurt so damn much - Wait, that's it? what did Sam actually do there? If Megatron wanted the allspice and all it took was that, why didn't he do that first?? - Ending scene: cuck car park None of this is to say I had a bad time though 🙂 It was great fun to watch a bit of a cornerstone of 2000s cinema and a part of many of my friends' personal canon. I wasn't there early enough, so I probably missed out - that's alright by me though.

I grew up watching Transformers as a kid, and I was completely into it. I had all the little robot toys, and I can still remember having fun transforming them and playing with them while watching the cartoon. So when this movie came out, there was definitely a part of me that was excited to see these characters brought to the big screen. And honestly, Transformers delivers pretty well on that childhood nostalgia. Seeing Optimus Prime, Bumblebee, Megatron, Starscream and the rest of the Transformers brought to life with modern special effects was pretty damn cool. The designs and transformations felt like a natural evolution of what I remembered from the cartoon, and the movie actually captures a lot of the spirit of what made the original series fun. Watching these giant robots transform, fight and tear up the screen is exactly the kind of thing younger me would have loved. As an adult, though, I can also see the movie’s flaws. The story isn’t anything groundbreaking, some of the human characters and comedy don’t always work for me, and at times it feels more like a showcase for the special effects than a great story. But I never really expected Transformers to be some deep cinematic experience. I wanted to have fun with it, and that’s exactly what I got. The action is entertaining, the effects still hold up pretty well, and there’s something satisfying about seeing characters I grew up with finally getting the big-budget treatment. Is it the best movie I’ve ever seen? Definitely not. Is it a bad movie? Not at all. For me, Transformers is simply a fun, nostalgic ride that brought a piece of my childhood back to the big screen.

Enjoyable movie. Shia Labeouf did a great job. I think his fidgety, anxious but courageous character is one of my favorite parts about this movie. Bumblebee and Optimus have awesome “aura” moments where they just steal the spotlight. Megatron as a villain is very interesting. The movie was a fun watch. The transformers were supposed to save the day and be the protectors. While they did do that, I think they learned just as much as the audience that HUMANS are not just going to be pushed around. Shia’s character is the sole example of why Optimus is fighting to save Earth. He is teaching the auto bots there is more that meets the eye. Cons, I think at times it seemed very fast paced. There are some moments that were hard to keep up with. The first half of the movie was very lackluster, the second half picks up a bit I did like the comedic relief in that half but what helps define this movie is the final act. Also it is hard to tell some of the robots apart. The biggest downside in my opinion is the lack of character depth to a lot of the robots and humans. In conclusion, the movie is a good watch. I think the cgi looks great even for today’s time. However, I personally believe there is a spark missing that could have made it better. 3/5
